title: Integration onramp: gateway adapter & SDK conversation - SummitWorks
summary: Exploratory discovery about integrating Redwood across SummitWorks' edge gateway and ML platform. Main threads: SDKs for server-side orchestration, LangChain/LlamaIndex connector patterns, gateway/proxy vs direct client calls, rate limiting and tenant quotas, and observability hooks. Customer is evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private for data residency and low-latency regional routing.
topics: Rate limits, quotas and per-tenant isolation
Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private tradeoffs
action_items: Alex: Share SDK quickstart repo and example gateway-adapter (due 2026-06-12)
Maya: Run a small perf baseline request pattern for SummitWorks test corpus and share numbers (due 2026-06-17)
Tom: Send sample traffic profile and SLOs (due 2026-06-14)
Priya: Provide list of compliance controls needed for Private deployment (no due date agreed)
next_steps: Send pricing options for Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private with egress and reserved capacity estimates
Schedule a technical deep dive / PoC kickoff next week to validate proxy adapter latency
Share security whitepaper and SOC2 checklist link
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-10 15:00 UTC
Duration: 49 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Tom Alvarez (SummitWorks CTO), Jenna Park (Lead ML Eng), Marco Li (Platform Eng), Priya Rao (Sec/Comp)

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro — Alex from Redwood, Maya our solutions engineer. How are you all doing?
[00:06] Tom Alvarez: Good, thanks. We wanted to map out integration options, mostly around our edge gateway and how Redwood would sit behind it.
[00:12] Jenna Park: Yeah, we've got a couple of generator workflows that run through our gateway, plus async embedding pipelines. Main goals are latency under 180ms p95 for small prompts and strong data isolation.
[00:22] Maya Patel: Got it. High-level, there are two common patterns we see: direct server-to-Redwood SDK calls from your microservices, or a thin gateway adapter/proxy that centralizes routing, caching, and quotas. Both can work with Hosted, Dedicated, or Private — just different tradeoffs.
[00:36] Marco Li: Can you elabor, like what the adapter would actually do? We already have an API gateway that handles tokens and rate limits.
[00:43] Alex Chen: Sure — typical adapter responsibilities: auth mapping (SAML token to Redwood API key), tenant mapping for per-tenant quotas, prefix/KV caching for repeated prompts, batching for throughput, and model routing policy. It can also emit observability hooks to your tracing and cost-analysis pipelines.
[01:00] Priya Rao: From security perspective, we need KMS integration and audit logs for every request. If we go Private, we also need offline deployable artifacts and HSM support.
[01:12] Maya Patel: We support customer-managed KMS for Private and Dedicated via our KMS integrations. Audit logs can stream to your SIEM — we can share the schema. For Hosted, we offer tenant-level audit and retention controls, but some customers prefer Private for strict residency.
[01:28] Jenna Park: About SDKs — we saw the JS and Python SDKs, any guidance for using them inside a gateway vs using the HTTP API directly?
[01:36] Maya Patel: SDKs give short helpers for batching, retry, and KV cache hooks; they also expose low-level streaming primitives. For a gateway adapter I usually recommend the lightweight Python SDK in async mode — easier to integrate with existing asyncio stacks. If you want polyglot, proxying HTTP is simpler but you lose some of the automations.
[01:53] Tom Alvarez: How does LangChain or LlamaIndex fit in? Our ML team uses LongChain extensively — sorry, LangChain — for orchestration.
[02:00] Maya Patel: Right — we have connector examples for LangChain and LlamaIndex. Most customers call Redwood via the SDK inside their chain nodes, or they create a custom proxy LLM wrapper that routes to Redwood and injects model hints or function-call templates. We can share a repo with LongChain/LlamaIndex examples.
[02:20] Marco Li: What about rate limits and quotas per tenant? Our gateway enforces per-customer QPS today. We need to ensure no noisy neighbor issues when traffic spikes.
[02:28] Alex Chen: Redwood has per-api-key quotas and token-based rate limits. With Dedicated you can get reserved capacity and per-tenant allocation at the pool level; with Hosted we offer per-api-key quota controls and throttles. If you centralize requests through an adapter, it's easier to implement per-tenant pooling and retry/backoff strategies.
[02:46] Jenna Park: Any options for burst behaviour? Some customers have spiky traffic during events.
[02:50] Maya Patel: Yes — Dedicated supports burst capacity and configured autoscaling policies. Hosted can do short bursts but sustained bursts above plan might be throttled; we can model your traffic and make recommendations.
[03:03] Tom Alvarez: Observability — we need token-level cost attribution and traces per request. How invasive is that to add?
[03:09] Alex Chen: We have an observability SDK that emits request-level metadata: tokens consumed, model version, latency, and error codes. It connects to common tracing backends via OpenTelemetry. You can enrich payloads in the adapter and forward spans to your tracer.
[03:24] Priya Rao: Is PII redaction supported in logs? We can't send raw user content to any third-party log store without masking.
[03:32] Maya Patel: You can configure prefix masking and redact fields before logging. For Private deployments you can keep logs entirely on-prem. In Hosted, we offer configurable retention and masking controls; we can walk through the whitepaper.
[03:47] Alex Chen: Quick note on caching: prefix caching and KV cache can reduce token cost significantly for repeated system prompts or conversational context. But caching interacts with privacy requirements — you may need stricter TTLs per tenant.
[04:00] Marco Li: If we implement cache in the adapter, what's the invalidation story? Our app sometimes updates the prompt templates.
[04:06] Maya Patel: We expose manual invalidation APIs and allow TTLs. Best practice is to version templates and evict by key on deploys.
[04:14] Tom Alvarez: Can you run the SDK inside a container in our gateway cluster, or do we need to call Redwood over the public internet?
[04:20] Alex Chen: Both possible. For Hosted & Dedicated, SDK/container will call our API endpoints over TLS. For Private you can run the inference runtime inside your VPC/on-prem and the control plane can be private. We'll share a diagram.
[04:33] Jenna Park: Model pinning and rollout — we like canarying. Does Redwood support A/B and automatic fallback?
[04:39] Maya Patel: Yes — rollouts are first class in the Console. You can do percent-based traffic shifts, canaries, and automatic fallback to previous model or a smaller variant if latency increases.
[04:49] [05:00] Speaker 1 (transcript noise): mm hm
[05:05] Marco Li: On performance: our cluster is in eu-west and we need p95 under 180ms for short prompts. Can you meet that with Hosted?
[05:12] Maya Patel: Depends on model and region. For smaller open models on eu-west instances, 150–220ms p95 is typical; but we'll run a tailored baseline with your payload. Dedicated or Private in your region gives the best predictability.
[05:29] Tom Alvarez: What's the effort to stand up Dedicated vs Private? Timeline and ops overhead?
[05:35] Alex Chen: Dedicated is quicker — reserved GPU pools in our cloud, provisioning around 2–4 weeks depending on capacity. Private (VPC or on-prem) needs network/config coordination, KMS/HSM, and O(4–8) weeks typically for on-prem. We'll provide the runbook.
[05:52] Jenna Park: Any concerns about kernel optimizations or model quantization? We run mixed workloads — embeddings and chat.
[05:58] Maya Patel: We support quantized variants for cost-sensitive inference and mixing model variants per route. The runtime selects kernels based on sequence length and hardware, which affects latency. For embeddings-heavy workloads we often recommend separate pools tuned for throughput.
[06:16] Marco Li: What about LangChain agents that call tools — will function calling be proxied cleanly?
[06:23] Maya Patel: Yes, function-calling and structured output are supported. The adapter can convert your tool calls into function schemas and route accordingly.
[06:32] Alex Chen: Quick real example — we had a customer who fronted Redwood with a go-based gateway adapter that did tenant throttling, OTel tracing and cached repeated FAQ prompts; they cut tokens by 30% and p95 latency improved.
[06:46] Tom Alvarez: Sounds promising. On pricing: do you price embeddings differently, and how are token counts measured for caching?
[06:53] Alex Chen: Embeddings are charged per vector unit; token accounting is per request on generated tokens. Caching reduces billed tokens only if you serve cached content instead of calling the model. We'll include example math in the pricing sheet.
[07:08] Jenna Park: For PoC we want a small pilot with one route proxied through a gateway adapter, and a baseline run against Hosted and Dedicated — compare latency/cost.
[07:16] Maya Patel: Great — that's straightforward. We'll need a sample prompt set and traffic pattern from you.
[07:21] Tom Alvarez: We'll send sample traffic and a list of SLOs by Monday.
[07:26] [07:30] Alex Chen: Action items recap — I'll send SDK samples and a small adapter repo link. Maya will produce a perf baseline for your corpus. We'll also share security docs and the SOC2 whitepaper.
[07:41] Priya Rao: Please include details on key rotation and HSM.
[07:46] Alex Chen: Will do. Any final questions?
[07:49] Jenna Park: One more — if we run embeddings pipeline asynchronously, can Redwood push webhooks when embeddings are ready or do we poll?
[07:58] Maya Patel: We offer async endpoints with webhook callbacks or polling depending on your infra. For high-throughput pipelines we recommend event-driven callbacks to reduce polling load.
[08:10] Tom Alvarez: Perfect. Let's schedule the PoC kickoff next week.
[08:14] Alex Chen: We'll follow up with calendar invite and docs. Thanks everyone.
[08:19] [meeting ends]
